Cache & sessions

Take the load your database hates

Sessions, rate limits, feature flags, the hot row every request reads. They are in Postgres in most applications, and they are the rows getting hammered — not because a database is bad at them, but because they were never questions. You already know the key.

Why this fits

Every one of these has the same shape: a key you already hold, a small value, and a lifetime. kevy does the lookup in O(1), expires the key itself without a cron job, and does several million of them a second on one machine.

The part people underrate is the expiry. A cache built on a database needs a sweeper, and the sweeper is where the bugs live. Here the engine drops the key when its time is up, whether or not anyone asks for it. Four tasks below — each one is pasteable into redis-cli against a running kevy.

And the long tail can outgrow RAM. With a RAM budget on ([tiering]), the coldest values spill to a disposable disk log and page back on access — every command unchanged on a cold key, durability untouched — so rarely-read sessions and archives stop costing RAM without a second store. Off by default; v1 spills strings and hashes. The tiering guide has the honest limits.

A session that cleans itself up

One key per session, gone by itself an hour after the last touch — no sweeper, no cron job, no expired-rows table.

  1. Write the session with its lifetime

    SET session:7f3a '{"user":"ada","role":"admin"}' EX 3600
-> OK

  2. Read it on every request

    GET session:7f3a
-> "{\"user\":\"ada\",\"role\":\"admin\"}"
TTL session:7f3a
-> (integer) 3599

  3. Sliding expiry: refresh on activity

    Touch the clock, not the value — the session dies one hour after the user goes quiet, not one hour after login.

    EXPIRE session:7f3a 3600
-> (integer) 1
Cost & limits

A session is one key, so every step here is O(1) and atomic. If you spread one user's state across several keys, atomicity ends at the shard — co-locate them with a {hashtag} in the key.

Rate-limit an endpoint

One counter per client per window; the 101st request inside a minute gets told no.

  1. Count the request

    INCR rate:203.0.113.7
-> (integer) 1

  2. Start the window on the first hit

    Only when the reply was 1 — later requests ride the window that already exists.

    EXPIRE rate:203.0.113.7 60
-> (integer) 1

  3. Refuse past the limit

    Your handler returns 429 when the counter passes the limit. The window keeps counting.

    INCR rate:203.0.113.7
-> (integer) 2      (the window survives)
Cost & limits

This is a fixed window, not a sliding one: a burst straddling the boundary can pass up to twice the limit in a short stretch. For abuse control that is fine and the whole thing is two O(1) commands; if you need smoother shaping, spend more keys, not a new system.

Feature flags, read on every request

All flags in one hash: one O(1) read on the hot path, one write to flip a flag for everyone.

  1. Set the flags

    HSET flags new-checkout on dark-mode on beta-search off
-> (integer) 3

  2. Read one on the hot path

    HGET flags new-checkout
-> "on"

  3. Flip one, everywhere, now

    HSET flags beta-search on
-> (integer) 0      (0 = updated, not added)
HGETALL flags
Cost & limits

One hash lives on one shard, so one shard answers every flag read. At flag-read rates that is still millions a second; if it ever becomes the hot spot, split the hash by surface or team.

Cache a row your database owns

The hot row served from memory; Postgres stays the truth and the copy can never outlive its backstop.

  1. On a read miss, fill with a backstop TTL

    SET user:881 "$json" EX 300
-> OK

  2. Serve reads from the copy

    GET user:881

  3. On write, invalidate — do not wait for the timer

    Delete after the database write commits. The next read misses, refills, and is correct.

    DEL user:881
-> (integer) 1
Cost & limits

A cache is a second copy of the truth, and it can be wrong — nothing solves that. Invalidate on write, not on a timer, and keep the TTL as the backstop rather than the plan. A multi-key DEL or MSET is atomic only within one shard: if two keys must change together, co-locate them with a {hashtag}.
